As you know, Mr Deputy Speaker, there was a debate that went until after two o'clock this morning in the other place about this bill. I want to make it very clear, firstly, that Labor believe that there was room to find longstanding reform in this area, and that is why we moved five separate amendments, including providing that the regulator for registered organisations be the Australian Securities and Investments Commission. The government reintroduced the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Bill to establish a Registered Organisations Commission, strengthen financial accountability, and introduce criminal penalties for union and employer organisation officers, citing misconduct including misuse of members' funds by the Health Services Union, National Union of Workers, and Transport Workers' Union.

The speaker moved to suspend standing orders to fast-track debate on the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Bill 2014, arguing it had been thoroughly scrutinised and passed by the House of Representatives three times previously before being rejected by the Senate. The motion proposed to limit debate by allowing one opposition speaker, then the Prime Minister to conclude before immediate votes on all remaining stages.

The speaker argued that the government's motion to gag debate on the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Bill 2014 prevents new MPs from speaking on one of the double dissolution trigger bills, and moved an amendment to allow a consideration in detail stage. They criticised the government and the Leader of the House for avoiding parliamentary debate on the legislation.

The Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Bill was reintroduced for the fourth time, with the government arguing it has a clear mandate following the double dissolution election to improve governance and accountability of unions and employer organisations, claiming the reforms will boost the economy rather than union-bust. The bill had been repeatedly blocked by the previous Senate and was cited as one of the two reasons for the July election.

Labor argued that the Senate's amendments to the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Bill 2014 were inadequate, proposing instead that ASIC be the regulator, whistleblower protections be expanded, auditor compliance be strengthened, donation disclosure thresholds be reduced to $1,000, and volunteers be exempted—all rejected by the government, leading Labor to oppose the bill.

The Turnbull government passed the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Bill 2014, establishing a Registered Organisations Commission with stronger enforcement powers and penalties to improve accountability and transparency for unions and employer groups. The speaker cited scandals involving Craig Thomson misusing $300,000 and Kathy Jackson fleecing over $1 million from the Health Services Union, and criticised Labor for opposing the reforms.

David Leyonhjelm The Family Tax Benefit (Tighter Income Test) Bill 2014 cuts government spending by more than $270 million a year by means-testing family tax benefit part A more rigorously. Both the coalition and Labor recognise that welfare payments should be means tested. This may seem an uncontroversial idea, but we should remember that some countries have welfare payments that are not means-tested, like universal age pensions, and we should remember that Labor have a troubled relationship with means-testing. They are proud of their changes in recent years to more rigorously means-test family payments and the private health insurance rebate, but they do not want to means-test access to Medicare, and they defend concessional loans for high-income beneficiaries of higher education. The coalition too have a troubled relationship with means-testing. They have loosened means-testing for the age pension and want the private health insurance rebate to be universal. And both sides have continued tied funding to the states that bans state owned hospitals and schools from imposing fees, even on high-income users of these services. Thanks to this inconsistency on means-testing, I have no great hope of support from either the coalition or Labor. But let me go through the process of making the case for the bill. Family tax benefit part A is a welfare payment. Do not be fooled by the mention of tax in the name. It goes to families regardless of whether or not they pay tax. Schedule 2 of the bill seeks to make significant changes to the way in which Australia will determine if it has protection obligations in relation to certain non-citizens. Specifically, the bill inserts a new section 6A that provides that a non-citizen is not entitled to complementary protection unless the person can prove that it is more likely than not that he or she will suffer significant harm if removed from Australia. Currently, the 'real chance' test means that a person must not be returned to a situation where there is a real chance that they would face significant harm. This means a chance which is not remote or insubstantial but which may be below 50 per cent and may be as low as 10 per cent. These changes have the potential to put vulnerable people seeking Australia's protection at risk of persecution, death or serious harm if returned to their country. While Labor notes that complementary protection applies to only a small cohort of those who apply for refugee status but are refused, they are nonetheless an important cohort. Introduced the Migration Amendment (Protection and Other Measures) Bill 2014, raising the threshold for non-refoulement protection claims from a 'real chance' of harm, which can be as low as a 10 per cent likelihood, to a 'more likely than not' standard requiring more than a 50 per cent chance, and repealing the 90-day rule in place since December 2005.

Opened remarks on the Migration Amendment (Protection and Other Measures) Bill 2014, noting there are around 52 million refugees or people of concern worldwide and arguing Australia cannot resettle them all, while marking the 41st anniversary of his own election to parliament.

Set out Labor's support for most of the Migration Amendment (Protection and Other Measures) Bill 2014, but opposed schedule 2's lowering of the complementary protection threshold to 'more likely than not' and schedule 4's item 17 removing automatic written tribunal decisions, saying Labor would move amendments to remove both provisions.

Supported the Migration Amendment (Protection and Other Measures) Bill 2014, noting the 2014 to 2015 humanitarian program will provide 11,000 of its 13,750 places for people needing resettlement from overseas, including 4,400 places this year for Christians fleeing persecution in Iraq and Syria.

Detailed Labor's opposition to schedule 2 of the Migration Amendment (Protection and Other Measures) Bill 2014, arguing its 'more likely than not' complementary protection test raises the risk threshold above 50 per cent, quoting the Refugee Council of Australia and commentator Tony Wright, who wrote that a 49 to 50 per cent chance of torture would be 'good enough' for the minister.

Supported the Migration Amendment (Protection and Other Measures) Bill 2014, crediting the government with freeing up 4,000 Special Humanitarian Program places last financial year and another 4,000 this year, and citing over 50 million people worldwide who would qualify as refugees as reason a strict, 12-provision selection process is needed.

Supported the Migration Amendment (Protection and Other Measures) Bill 2014, arguing the complementary protection threshold should rise from around ten per cent to 50 per cent, and recounted meeting the UNHCR and IOM in Sri Lanka regarding 43 people who returned home after claiming persecution, most of them Sinhalese rather than minority Tamils.

Opposed schedule 2 of the Migration Amendment (Protection and Other Measures) Bill 2014, arguing its shift from a 'real chance' to a 'more likely than not' threshold for complementary protection abandons established case law and could see people returned to serious harm, quoting law academic Jane McAdam and the Refugee Council of Australia.

Supported the Migration Amendment (Protection and Other Measures) Bill 2014, noting Australia's ratio of working-age to over-65 Australians has fallen from 10 to one in 1965, to five to one today, and is projected to reach 2.8 to one by 2050, and argued establishing identity should be a basic requirement for asylum claims.

Supported the Migration Amendment (Protection and Other Measures) Bill 2014, attributing the processing backlog partly to the arrival of more than 800 boats and 50,000 people, and citing an estimated $12 billion policy cost under the previous government's border protection failures.

Opposed the Migration Amendment (Protection and Other Measures) Bill 2014, arguing its complementary protection threshold change means a person found only 49 per cent likely to be executed on return could still be denied protection, and said the bill's onus-of-proof and documentation provisions breach Australia's non-refoulement obligations.

Supported the Migration Amendment (Protection and Other Measures) Bill 2014, citing an $11.5 billion cost blow-out in border protection under the previous government against $2.5 billion in savings since, and noting the number of children in immigration detention has fallen by more than 40 per cent.

Accused the Coalition of hypocrisy for blocking Labor's Malaysia people-swap agreement and later opposing the Papua New Guinea resettlement arrangement, arguing that six hundred and eighty-nine people subsequently died at sea as a result, and credited the Papua New Guinea agreement with the greatest reduction yet in boat arrivals.

Supported the Migration Amendment (Protection and Other Measures) Bill 2014, arguing that stronger identity checks, consequences for fraudulent documents, clearer applicant responsibilities and more efficient review procedures would protect the integrity of Australia's humanitarian and protection visa systems while preserving assistance for genuinely vulnerable people.

Summed up the Migration Amendment (Protection and Other Measures) Bill, saying it would improve the integrity and efficiency of protection processing by clarifying applicants' responsibilities, strengthening identity requirements, applying a 'more likely than not' threshold to complementary protection, streamlining statutory bars and improving tribunal administration.

Opposed the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Bill as an ideological attack on unions, arguing it imposes harsher penalties on union officers than company directors face, and recalled WorkChoices-era cases including Optus contractors facing $300 a week pay cuts and $12,000 van costs.

Supported the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Bill for greater transparency, citing the Victorian construction industry royal commission's allegations of nepotism, blackmail and cartel behaviour against the CFMEU, and criticised Labor for not distancing itself from the union.

Closed debate on the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Bill, explaining the new Registered Organisations Commission would both educate officials on their duties and prosecute deliberate noncompliance, with penalty provisions modelled on the Corporations Act.

Noted the coalition strongly opposed, in February, a Labor proposal to restrict the research and development tax credit for companies with turnover above $20 billion, but is now bringing forward the identical savings measure in December.

Supported the Tax Laws Amendment (Research and Development) Bill 2013, citing Cochlear as an Australian innovation success story with around $800 million in sales and more than $100 million reinvested annually in research, and noted the $1.8 billion research and development tax incentive forms part of $8.9 billion in total Commonwealth innovation spending announced for 2012-13.

Supported restricting the R&D tax incentive to companies with less than $20 billion in domestic turnover to fund Labor's $1 billion Plan for Australian Jobs, accused the coalition of taking the savings while abandoning the plan as a broken promise, and noted the automotive industry, which employs 50,000 people directly and 200,000 indirectly, performs 25 per cent of manufacturing R&D.

Supported restricting the R&D tax offset to companies with less than $20 billion turnover to fund Labor's jobs plan, citing more than 950,000 jobs created between 2007 and 2013 and Job Services Australia finding work for 1.5 million Australians since 2009, and criticised the Queensland government's plan to close 40 per cent of TAFE campuses.

Opposed the R&D tax incentive bill limiting the offset to companies with less than $20 billion income, affecting 15 to 20 firms and saving an estimated $1.1 billion over four years, arguing the coalition kept the savings but scrapped Labor's related $500 million plan for 10 industry-innovation precincts and $350 million innovation investment fund round.

Supported the Tax Laws Amendment (Research and Development) Bill better targeting R&D tax incentives to smaller, more responsive firms, but noted the coalition, through then spokesperson Sophie Mirabella, had opposed the identical measure before the election.

Opposed the R&D tax bill, warning it would push R&D offshore and hurt small businesses, and noted Australia's ranking on the Global Innovation Index fell from 18th in 2010 to 23rd in 2012 while public R&D spending risks dropping to two per cent of GDP, well short of the Greens' proposed three per cent target.

Closed debate rejecting Labor's amendments, which would have restored R&D tax incentives for companies with more than $20 billion in turnover, and defended limiting the incentive from 1 July 2013 to smaller firms to save an estimated $1.1 billion toward paying down Labor's $430-plus billion debt.

Criticised Labor for blocking budget repair in the Senate, warning gross debt is projected to reach $499 billion by 2023-24 costing $14 billion a year in interest, and said scrapping the carbon tax and lower interest rates are saving the average family $190 a month while over 200,000 jobs were created last year.
